slides.title: One slow API took the whole site down
slides.tldr: When the courier API slows down, it is not just checkout that dies. The whole site stops, because every worker is stuck waiting for its reply.

blocks.title: A pizza place with 20 waiters
blocks.body: A restaurant has 20 waiters. Today the pizza oven is broken, and one pizza takes half an hour. Every waiter who takes a pizza order ends up standing at the counter, waiting. Soon all 20 are standing there, and a customer who only wants a glass of water can't get anyone to bring it. On your server the waiters are PHP-FPM **workers** (the processes that each handle one request at a time), and the broken oven is the courier API.

blocks.caption: The courier API is slow, and in 10 seconds the whole site is dead

nodes.label: Users
nodes.tip: Not everyone is checking out. Most people are just browsing products, yet all of them will suffer.

nodes.label: App server
nodes.tip: A worker handles one request at a time. 20 workers means at most 20 requests in flight together.

nodes.label: Courier API
nodes.tip: It is not down, just slow. So the connection succeeds, but the reply comes very late.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: The database is blameless and its CPU is nearly idle. The problem is somewhere else.

edges.label: 2 checkout requests arrive every second
Each checkout asks the courier for a delivery charge
The reply arrives 30 seconds later, and the worker is stuck until then
2 × 10 = 20: within ten seconds every worker is stuck
edges.tip: Two more workers get stuck every second, and none is released before the 30 seconds are up.

edges.label: The database sits idle, but there is no free worker to call it
Even home page requests now get a 504
edges.tip: nginx finds no free worker, waits, and finally returns 504 Gateway Timeout.

blocks.body: A slow service is more dangerous than a dead one: it never says "no" right away, it just keeps your workers hostage.

aside.title: Sale-day afternoon
aside.body: On a sale day, an online shop's courier API slowed down. The team checked: database fine, server CPU only 10%, and yet the site wouldn't load. The CPU wasn't busy because the workers were just sitting and waiting. Waiting costs no CPU, but it does cost a worker.

items.meaning: A server process that takes one request and handles it to the end. There is only a limited number of them.
Anything your code relies on: an external API, the database, a cache, another service.
The front server (nginx) did not get a reply from the app behind it in time.

check.q: The courier API is slow, so why does a user who is only viewing the home page get an error too?
check.a: The checkout requests are holding every worker while they wait for the courier. No free worker is left to handle the home page request.

slides.title: How failure spreads, and where to build walls
slides.tldr: A cascading failure spreads through shared, limited resources. Two walls stop it: timeouts and bulkheads.

blocks.body: When a problem in one place drags healthy parts down one after another, it is called a **cascading failure**. The trick is always the same: the sick part grabs a limited resource that everyone shares, such as workers, database connections, memory or a queue.

blocks.caption: Five steps from one slow dependency to a whole system down

steps.title: 1. One dependency slows
steps.body: The courier API takes 30 seconds instead of 200 ms.
steps.tip: It always starts small: one slow query, one slow external service, one full disk.

steps.title: 2. Workers get stuck waiting
steps.body: Every worker that calls it sits and waits for the reply.
steps.tip: Without a timeout, this wait never ends. The first wall goes up here.

steps.title: 3. The pool runs out
steps.body: All 20 workers are taken. New requests pile up in line.
steps.tip: Because the resource is shared, one feature eats everyone's share. The second wall goes up here.

steps.title: 4. Healthy features die
steps.body: Home, login, search: nothing to do with the courier, yet all down.
steps.tip: To the user the whole site is now down, even though only one small part is broken.

steps.title: 5. It spreads upward
steps.body: Whoever calls your API gets stuck waiting for you too.
steps.tip: Mobile apps, other services, even retries pile on more load, and the failure climbs one level up.

blocks.title: The two walls
items: **Timeout** (at step 2): never wait forever for a call. When the time is up, the worker is freed.
**Bulkhead** (at step 3): give each dependency its own share of the resource. When one share runs out, the others stay intact.

blocks.body: Failure travels along whatever resource everyone shares.

items.meaning: One part's failure knocking over the other parts one by one, like dominoes.
The separate compartments in a ship's hull. If one floods, the others stay dry and the ship floats.
A ready-made, limited stock of a resource, such as 20 workers or 50 database connections.

aside.body: The restaurant's two rules: a waiter never stands more than 2 minutes (timeout), and no more than 5 people at the oven counter at once (bulkhead).

items.label: The third wall: the circuit breaker

check.q: At which two of the five steps can you build a wall, and with what?
check.a: At step 2 with a timeout, so workers don't wait forever. At step 3 with a bulkhead, so one dependency can't take every worker and the other features survive.

slides.title: Put a timeout on every network call
slides.tldr: Give HttpClient both timeout (idle) and max_duration (total), set statement_timeout on the database, and write down in code what happens on failure.

blocks.body: The restaurant rule: a waiter never stands at the counter for more than 2 minutes, and if the pizza isn't ready, goes back and tells the customer. In code, make a separate **scoped client** (an HTTP client preconfigured for one service) for each dependency and give it two clocks. Set the values just above that service's normal slowest reply (p99, the time 99% of calls beat).

blocks.code:
framework:
    http_client:
        default_options:
            timeout: 3          # idle: give up if nothing arrives for this many seconds
            max_duration: 10    # maximum time for the whole call
        scoped_clients:
            courier.client:
                base_uri: 'https://api.courier.example'
                timeout: 2
                max_duration: 4

marks.tip: timeout is the idle timeout: no more than this much silence is tolerated between two chunks of data. If you don't set it, the default is 60 seconds.
max_duration is the total limit for request plus response. If you don't set it, there is no limit at all.
Each external service gets its own client with its own limits. A slow reporting API and a fast courier API should not share limits.
Because the argument is named $courierClient, Symfony injects the scoped client called courier.client here.
HttpClient is lazy: the timeout exception is thrown not in request() but when you read the response (toArray). So the read must be inside the try too.
Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface covers timeouts, failed connections, 4xx/5xx responses and broken JSON.

blocks.caption: Which timeout goes where, and a starting value

rows.tip: The two clocks of Symfony HttpClient. Pick the values from that API's p99 latency, not by guessing.
If a query runs longer than this, the database cancels it itself. Set it on the web app's database user.
How long to wait for another transaction to release its lock. Without it, the wait is unbounded.
A cache is supposed to be fast. If it is slow, don't wait for it: read from the database.
PHP-FPM's last line of defense: past this limit it kills the worker and starts a fresh one.

blocks.body: Every network call gets a timeout. No exceptions.

items.desc: No query from the web database user may run longer than 5 seconds
Wait at most 2 seconds for a lock
See the current value (0 means no limit)

items: Inner timeouts are always shorter than the outer ones: HttpClient 4 s < PHP-FPM 30 s < nginx 35 s.
Keep a separate database user for reports or migrations, with longer limits.

items.label: How to split a timeout budget

check.q: If HttpClient only has timeout: 3, what kind of slow server can still hold a worker for minute after minute?
check.a: One that dribbles out a little data every 1-2 seconds. The silence between two chunks never reaches 3 seconds, so the idle timeout never fires. You need max_duration to bound the total time.

slides.title: Bulkheads: a separate compartment for each job
slides.tldr: Stop one dependency from taking every worker or the whole queue: cap the number of simultaneous calls, and keep separate queues and workers per job type.

blocks.body: Even with a 4-second timeout, 5 checkouts a second (5 × 4 = 20) still stick all 20 workers. So the restaurant's second rule: at most 5 waiters at the oven counter at once, and the sixth doesn't wait but tells the customer straight away. In code, Symfony's **Semaphore** does this: a counted set of tokens that limits how many can enter at the same time.

blocks.caption: The same 20 workers, unshared and shared

columns.title: Everyone in one pool
items: Courier slows and all 20 workers are stuck
Payment messages wait behind 5,000 reports
An admin's heavy export eats customers' workers
columns.tip: The slow job gradually eats the whole pool, leaving nothing for the others.

columns.title: In separate compartments
items: At most 5 workers for the courier, 15 always free
payments, emails, reports: three separate queues and workers
A separate PHP-FPM pool for admins
columns.tip: Each job has its own limit. When one compartment floods, only that feature suffers.

marks.tip: limit 5: a semaphore with this name never admits more than 5 at once. ttl 10 seconds: even if a worker dies, the slot frees itself.
acquire() doesn't wait. If there is no room it returns false immediately. That is exactly what we want: fail fast.
If you don't release in finally, after an exception the slot stays taken until the ttl runs out.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        transports:
            payments:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                options: { queue_name: payments }
            emails:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                options: { queue_name: emails }
            reports:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                options: { queue_name: reports }
        routing:
            App\Message\CapturePayment: payments
            App\Message\SendOrderEmail: emails
            App\Message\BuildSalesReport: reports

marks.tip: queue_name is an option of the Doctrine transport. On Redis you would use a stream, and on AMQP a separate queue name.
Payment messages go to their own queue. However long the report line grows, this one is unaffected.

aside.title: Each queue gets its own workers

items.desc: Payment jobs only, for example 4 processes

items: To enable Symfony Semaphore: composer require symfony/semaphore, then give framework.semaphore a Redis DSN.
Send admin and report URLs to a separate PHP-FPM pool (its own pm.max_children) so heavy exports can't eat customers' workers.
Size the compartments by arithmetic: the sum of all of them should stay below the total number of workers.
Too low a limit turns healthy calls away. Calls per second × normal reply time, plus headroom: 5 × 0.2 s = 1, so 5 slots is plenty.

check.q: A 4-second timeout is set. Why can the site still go down when the courier is slow, and how does a bulkhead prevent it?
check.a: With 5 checkouts a second, all 20 workers are stuck within 4 seconds. A semaphore gives the courier at most 5 workers, so the other 15 stay free for everything else.

slides.title: Pitfall: "there is a default timeout anyway"
slides.tldr: The defaults are either 60 seconds or unlimited. And PHP's max_execution_time doesn't count time spent waiting on the network.

blocks.body: This is how we call outside APIs in a CRUD app, and we assume PHP's 30-second limit will save us. But on Linux, `max_execution_time` counts only the time PHP code is actually running. Time spent waiting for a network or database reply is not counted. So the worker below can stay stuck for 60 seconds or even longer.

marks.tip: Without a timeout, the idle limit is PHP's default_socket_timeout = 60 seconds, and there is no limit on total time at all.
If the courier fails, the exception goes straight to the user as a 500. Nobody thought about what should happen on failure.
The limits now come from courier.client, so a stuck call ends after 4 seconds at most instead of holding the worker for a minute.
The response is read inside the try, so a timeout lands in the catch and the user gets a default charge, not a 500.

blocks.caption: The limits you get if you change nothing

cells: One call can hold a worker for a minute
rows.tip: The default comes from PHP's default_socket_timeout. Twenty slow calls a minute are enough to jam 20 workers.
A server that sends data bit by bit never trips the idle timeout.
On Linux only the script's own running time counts. Time spent in streams, database queries or sleep is excluded.

cells: A slow query can run for hours
rows.tip: One bad query holds a database connection until someone kills it by hand.
This is the only limit that counts real wall-clock time and forcibly stops the worker.

blocks.title: Three fixes
items: Set both `timeout` and `max_duration` on every scoped client, as in the previous slide.
Keep the whole call, including reading the response, inside try/catch, and decide what to return on failure.
Set `request_terminate_timeout = 30s` in PHP-FPM: it is the last net if everything else misses.
Too short a timeout makes a healthy service look failed; too long makes it useless. Measure p99 and choose from that.
A timeout doesn't mean the work didn't happen. For calls like payments, the outcome is unknown.

aside.body: Defaults are written so nothing breaks, not to protect your site. Write the limits yourself.

items.label: After a timeout: "did it happen or not?"

check.q: php.ini has max_execution_time = 30, yet a worker stayed stuck on the courier API for 60 seconds. How?
check.a: On Linux, max_execution_time doesn't count time spent waiting on the network. With no timeout set on HttpClient, default_socket_timeout (60 seconds) was the only limit.

slides.title: Let everyone in, and nobody gets served
slides.tldr: When more requests arrive than you can handle, an unbounded line keeps growing and replies come after the user has left. The server works hard and achieves nothing.

blocks.title: The ticket counter before Thanksgiving
blocks.body: One clerk sits at the counter, and each ticket takes a fixed amount of time. People join the line faster than she can serve them, and nobody is ever turned away. The line grows until the person who finally gets a ticket has already missed the train. The clerk worked all day, yet helped no one. On your server the counter is a worker, the line is a queue, and the train's departure is the user's timeout.

blocks.caption: 60 requests a second arrive, 50 can be served: the line never shrinks, it only grows

nodes.label: Users
nodes.tip: A sudden crowd on sale day. Users wait at most 30 seconds, then hit refresh or leave.

nodes.label: Waiting line
nodes.tip: nginx's backlog, PHP-FPM's line or a Messenger queue: all of them are lines. Without a limit, they grow as much as they like.

nodes.label: App server
nodes.tip: Capacity is fixed. The server does not suddenly get faster because the crowd got bigger.

edges.label: 60 requests a second join the line
The server takes 50 a second, so the line grows by 10 every second
After 10 minutes there are 6,000 in line: replies take 120 seconds
edges.tip: 6,000 ÷ 50 = 120 seconds. Users gave up after 30 seconds, so nobody ever sees these replies.

blocks.body: Let in more work than you can handle and it is not that everyone gets slower. Everyone fails.

aside.title: A busy server, zero results
aside.body: On campaign day, an e-commerce site's CPU sat at 100%: the server was working at full capacity every second. Yet almost no orders went through. The replies were being written to connections the clients had already closed. The server was busy, but nothing was getting done.

items.meaning: More work arriving at once than the system can handle.
The rate of replies users actually received in time. Count results, not busyness.

check.q: The server is 100% busy, yet users say the site isn't working. How is that possible?
check.a: The line is so long that replies arrive after the user's timeout. The server is handling requests whose reader is gone, so goodput is close to zero.

slides.title: Keep the line short and turn the rest away at once
slides.tldr: Load shedding means turning away requests above your limit at the door. The rest get full-speed service, and those turned away know when to come back.

blocks.title: A "tickets sold out" sign at the gate
blocks.body: A good station clerk steps out and announces: "We have 50 tickets today. Everyone else, please come back tomorrow." Those who got in received their tickets on time, and those turned away didn't waste their day. That is **load shedding**: deliberately refusing the work you can't handle.

A line with a maximum length is a **bounded queue**. Once it is full, new requests get a 503 immediately. This is how a step further along tells the step before it "I'm full, send slower", which is called **back-pressure**. Rejecting a request costs almost nothing, while letting it in and timing it out later costs a lot.

blocks.caption: Limit 50: the first 50 get in, the other 10 are turned back at once

nodes.label: Users
nodes.tip: The crowd is the same as before. The difference is that the server now knows its limit.

nodes.label: The gate
nodes.tip: A rate limiter or bounded queue. It counts how many are inside and lets no more in once the limit is reached.

nodes.label: App server
nodes.tip: There is no line now, so every request gets to work straight away.

edges.label: 60 requests a second reach the gate
The first 50 get in and are handled at full speed
The other 10 instantly get a 503 with Retry-After: 2
edges.tip: Turning someone away is not the same as failing them: the client knows to try again in 2 seconds.

edges.label: The 50 that got in are answered in 200 ms

blocks.caption: Which status code to use when turning requests away, and why

cells: This client is asking too much
rows.tip: 429 is personal: one user or API key went over its limit. 503 is for everyone: the whole system is overloaded.
Even a sleepy server at night will return 429 to one client asking too much. 503 only when the server is really struggling.
Send a Retry-After header in both cases, or clients will guess when to retry and add to the crowd.

blocks.body: Saying "no" at the door is cheaper and politer than timing someone out after they got in.

items.meaning: A full step telling the step before it to slow down, so the crowd doesn't pile up behind it.
A queue with a fixed maximum size. When it is full, new items are not let in.
An HTTP header saying how many seconds to wait before trying again.

aside.body: A line with no limit is not a line, it is a pit. Hit the limit and say "no" at once.

use: Demand above capacity, whether a sudden sale crowd or a viral link
Work the client can safely retry later
avoid: A brief burst that a short bounded queue can absorb
Clients that cannot retry, like a one-shot webhook with no retries

check.q: Doesn't turning some users away make the site look bad? Why is it still better?
check.a: Without it, everyone would wait 120 seconds and fail. With it, 50 people are served fast and the rest know right away when to come back.

slides.title: Cap the less important work first with Symfony RateLimiter
slides.tldr: A token bucket caps low-priority routes at a fixed rate and answers 503 with Retry-After when it is hit. It is a budget, not yet shedding: it ignores how busy the server is.

blocks.body:
Not all requests are equally important. In a crowd, shed things like search, recommendations and reports first, to save room for checkout and payment. Below is a token bucket (a bucket that refills with tokens at a steady rate): a fixed budget of at most 50 low-priority requests per second, with one shared key (`global`) for everyone.

Be clear about what this is: a cap that never looks at the server. It refuses request 51 even when the server is idle, so it is a budget, not yet load shedding. The next slide makes it react.

blocks.code:
framework:
    rate_limiter:
        low_priority:
            policy: 'token_bucket'
            limit: 100            # at most 100 tokens in the bucket (tolerates small bursts)
            rate: { interval: '1 second', amount: 50 }   # refills 50 tokens every second

marks.tip: From the name low_priority, Symfony autowiring creates the argument name $lowPriorityLimiter.
limit is the size of the bucket: a sudden burst of 100 is tolerated, but the sustained rate cannot exceed 50 a second.
priority 30: it runs before the firewall, so shed requests don't even pay the cost of authentication.
The shedding list is written out plainly: which paths can be sacrificed, decided in advance.
A shed request ends right here. It costs nothing at the controller, the database or any external API.

blocks.title: What to shed first
items: First of all: reports, exports, anything that can be pushed to the background
Then: search, recommendations, live counters. The site works without them
Last: browsing. Shed it and users leave the site
Never: payment, checkout, login, health checks
Keep the shedding list short: 3-4 paths are enough, and a longer list raises the risk of shedding the wrong path.
First only log how many requests would have been shed, then switch it on. A limit set by guesswork will shed healthy traffic.
To share the overall limit across several servers, give the limiter Redis as its cache pool. Otherwise each server counts separately.

use: To protect less important routes when a crowd suddenly arrives
As a safety net before a campaign or sale
avoid: With numbers you set without measuring
As your only defense: it never checks whether the server is struggling

check.q: Why is the shedding listener placed on kernel.request instead of in a controller?
check.a: A shed request never reaches the controller, the database or external APIs. So shedding costs almost nothing, and the capacity it saves goes to the important work.

slides.title: Make it react: shed only while the server is struggling
slides.tldr: A fixed cap refuses people even when the server is idle. Check an overload signal first, and enforce the cap only while the server is really struggling.

blocks.body: Picture 3 a.m.: the server is 10% busy, 80 searches a second arrive, and the cap is 50. Thirty people a second are refused for nothing, like a clerk shouting "sold out" with half the tickets still in the drawer. Real shedding starts only when the server says "I'm struggling". So the listener first asks an overload signal, and applies the cap only if the answer is yes.

blocks.caption: The same cap, with and without a check on how the server is doing

columns.title: Fixed cap only
items: 3 a.m., server 10% busy, 80 searches a second: 30 refused for nothing
The cap is the same whether the server is at 10% or at 100%
columns.tip: The cap is a number someone guessed. It never asks how the server feels.

columns.title: Cap + overload signal
items: 3 a.m.: the signal says healthy, all 80 searches are served
Sale day: the signal says overloaded, the cap of 50 applies, the rest get 503
Checkout and payment are never on the list, in either case
columns.tip: The signal decides when to refuse. The cap only decides how much still gets through.

columns.title: What it costs
items: Load average is a 1-minute average, so shedding starts late and stops late
Each server judges only itself: one can shed while its neighbor sits idle
Not needed if demand always stays far below capacity
columns.tip: Every recommendation has a price. Know it before you copy the code.

marks.tip: About 1 task per core means the CPU is fully used. 1.5 per core means work is queueing for a core.
The new gate: while the server is healthy, the listener returns here and the cap is never consulted.
Only an overloaded server reaches the bucket. Inside the 50 a second budget a request still passes; the rest get 503.

blocks.body: A cap that never looks at the server is a budget. Shedding starts when the server says it is struggling.

items: The 1.5 × cores line is a starting guess. Log the load average during a normal busy hour, then set the line above it.
If requests mostly wait on a database or an API, the CPU stays calm while requests pile up. Count in-flight requests or queue depth instead.
Keep the detector behind its own class, so you can swap load average for queue depth or slow replies later.

items.meaning: How many tasks, averaged over the last minute, were running or waiting for a CPU core. About the number of cores means fully busy.
A number you can read in an instant that says the server is struggling: load average, busy workers, queue depth, slow replies.

check.q: At 3 a.m. the server is idle but 80 searches a second arrive and the cap is 50. What does a fixed cap do, and what does the overload check change?
check.a: A fixed cap refuses 30 a second for nothing. With the check, nobody is refused while the server is healthy; the cap applies only once it reports overload.

slides.title: Pitfall: "just put it in the queue, it'll get done later"
slides.tldr: An unbounded queue hides a crowd, it does not solve it. The line grows for hours and workers process stale jobs. Measure queue depth and return 503 at the limit.

blocks.body: In a CRUD app our habit is to push heavy work onto a queue and return `202 Accepted`. But when messages arrive faster than the workers can process them, the queue grows every minute. An hour later, the user who asked for one report has asked ten more times. All of them sit in the queue, and the workers keep producing that stale work.

marks.tip: However long the queue is, new work gets in. The wait stretches from hours to days.
202 means "received", not "we will do it". It makes no promise about when.
The Doctrine, Redis and AMQP transports implement MessageCountAwareInterface. The in-memory and sync transports do not.
getMessageCount() now counts waiting messages. 500 is this queue's limit: if the worker clears 100 a minute, nobody waits more than 5 minutes.

blocks.body: Every queue gets a maximum depth, and once it is reached, new work is turned away.

items: Set the limit from the worker's speed: limit ÷ jobs handled per minute = longest wait. Ask whether users can tolerate that wait.
A limit alone is not enough: if a job has gone stale, check its age in the handler and drop it, or workers will build outdated results.
To protect the server itself, set pm.max_children in php-fpm and a sensible timeout in nginx, so one request can't take another's place.

items.label: Giving something instead of turning people away

check.q: The queue limit is 500 and the worker finishes 100 a minute. At the limit, what is the longest wait for the last message to get in?
check.a: 500 ÷ 100 = 5 minutes. Set your limit by doing this sum: the wait should stay within what users will tolerate, otherwise lower the limit.

slides.title: When everyone retries at once, the service can't get back up
slides.tldr: In a partial failure, if everyone retries immediately, traffic grows and a recovering service falls over again. This is called a retry storm.

blocks.title: Redialling a busy hotline
blocks.body: The electricity office hotline is busy. Everyone thinks, "It didn't connect, I'll dial again," and keeps pressing redial every second. The line gets even more crowded, and people with a real emergency can't get through either. In code, that redial is a retry. When everyone does it at the same moment, it becomes a **retry storm**.

A service doesn't always go down completely. Often it is in a **partial failure**: say, 50 out of every 100 calls to the payment gateway are failing. Now each of your failed calls immediately retries 3 more times. The numbers below show the result.

blocks.caption: Capacity is 150 a second: without retries 100, with 3 retries about 190

items.label: Normal traffic
items.tip: One attempt per call. The gateway handles this easily.

items.label: Gateway capacity
items.tip: Send more than this and the gateway fails even more. This limit is the real constraint.

items.label: With 3 retries
items.tip: 100 × (1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125) ≈ 190. If 50% fail, half of the calls at each step try again.

blocks.body: Sending more requests to a failing service just drowns it further.

aside.title: The service that could not recover
aside.body: A payment gateway slowed down for a few seconds. Every app retried at once, and traffic tripled. The gateway never got the chance to recover and stayed failing for an hour. The original problem would have been over in a minute; the retries turned it into an hour-long one.

items.meaning: The service is not fully down: some requests fail or are slow. The hardest state to handle.
Many clients resending failed calls at once, multiplying the load on the service.

check.q: The gateway is failing 50% of calls. If you add 3 immediate retries, roughly how many times more traffic is that, and what follows?
check.a: About 1.9 times. Traffic above capacity makes the gateway fail even more, which triggers more retries, and it never gets a chance to recover.

slides.title: Circuit breaker: protecting the house like a fuse
slides.tldr: A circuit breaker counts failed calls. At the threshold it stops calling altogether (open), later tries one test call (half-open), and on success switches back on (closed).

blocks.title: The circuit breaker at home
blocks.body: When the wiring shorts, the circuit breaker in your electrical panel cuts the line by itself so a fire doesn't start. After a while you gently flip the switch back: if all is well it keeps running, and if it shorts again it trips immediately. In code, that is exactly a circuit breaker: the healthy state is **closed**, the cut state is **open**, and the testing state is **half-open**.

blocks.caption: The three states of a circuit breaker and the four transitions

nodes.label: CLOSED
nodes.tip: The normal state. Every call goes to the service, and the breaker quietly counts failures.

nodes.label: OPEN
nodes.tip: Calls return at once (fail fast) with a fallback answer. The load on the service is zero.

nodes.label: HALF-OPEN
nodes.tip: One call (or a very few) is let through to see whether the service has recovered. Not all of them, so it isn't flooded again.

edges.label: 5 failures in a row
edges.tip: At the threshold the fuse trips. The threshold is set by a number of failures or a percentage.

edges.label: after 30 seconds
edges.tip: The service is given time to recover. Not a single call goes through meanwhile.

edges.label: test succeeds
edges.tip: The call came back fine, so the fuse is switched back on.

edges.label: test fails
edges.tip: It hasn't recovered yet. Cut again for 30 seconds, nothing gets through.

blocks.body: A breaker's job is not to prevent failure but to **reduce the cost of failure**: while open, a worker doesn't sit waiting out a 2-second timeout, it returns a fallback answer immediately. And the service gets a rest.
When a service is sick, stop calling it, and test it in small doses to see when it is better.

items.meaning: When you know a call will fail, say so immediately instead of waiting.
How many failures it takes before the breaker trips: for example 5 in a row, or a 50% rate.

aside.body: CLOSED runs, OPEN is cut, HALF-OPEN is a test: on success it switches back on, otherwise it is cut again.

use: Calls to a remote service that can hang or fail: payment gateway, courier, SMS
avoid: Calls inside your own process: nothing to protect
Tiny traffic: 5 failures in a row may take hours. Price: users get the fallback while it is open

check.q: The breaker is OPEN. A user presses checkout. What does their request get, and what does the gateway get?
check.a: The user gets a fallback answer immediately, with no timeout wait. The gateway gets no call at all, so it is free of load and can recover.

slides.title: How to retry properly: backoff and jitter
slides.tldr: Wait longer before each retry (exponential backoff), and add a little randomness to that wait (jitter). Symfony RetryableHttpClient does both from config.

blocks.body: The hotline mistake was redialling again and again at once. The right way: wait a little the first time, then double it, then double again. That is **exponential backoff**. But if everyone comes back at the exact same moment, you get another crowd, so add a bit of randomness to each wait. That is **jitter**.

blocks.code:
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            payment.client:
                base_uri: 'https://api.gateway.example'
                timeout: 2
                max_duration: 6
                retry_failed:
                    max_retries: 3
                    delay: 500          # 500 ms before the first retry
                    multiplier: 2       # doubles each time: 500, 1000, 2000
                    max_delay: 4000     # never more than 4 seconds, however large it gets
                    jitter: 0.3         # ±30% randomness
                    http_codes: [429, 502, 503, 504]

marks.tip: max_retries 3 means 4 attempts in all: the first one and 3 retries. The more repeated calls, the more load on the gateway.
jitter: 0.3 varies each wait by up to 30% either way, so clients don't all return at the same instant.
Retry only temporary errors. 400, 404 and 422 mean the call itself is wrong, and sending it a hundred times won't fix it.
Because the argument is named $paymentClient, Symfony injects the scoped client payment.client, retries included.
Retrying means the same call may go out more than once. The danger is a POST without a key: charged twice. With a key, the gateway recognizes the second one.

blocks.caption: Wait times over three retries: 500 ms, doubling, jitter ±30%

rows.tip: Starts from delay: 500. With 30% jitter, any value in this range can occur.
multiplier: 2, so double the previous one. The wait grows each time, giving the service more time.
max_delay is 4,000, so this is still under the cap. With more retries it would stop at 4 seconds.

blocks.body: Retry with growing waits (backoff), with randomness (jitter), and only on temporary errors.

items: Where a user is waiting, total time = attempts × timeout + waits. Here that is 4 × 2 + 3.5 = 11.5 seconds, so use fewer retries.
Retry only safe or idempotent calls: GET, and POST only with an Idempotency-Key.
Backoff without jitter makes all clients return together, and the crowd arrives in repeated waves (a thundering herd).
Retry is not a substitute for a timeout. Every attempt needs its own timeout.

check.q: Backoff but no jitter: what happens when 1,000 clients fail together, and what does jitter change?
check.a: They all return after exactly 500 ms, then 1000 ms, sending 1,000 calls at once in repeated waves. Jitter spreads those calls out over time and flattens the waves.

slides.title: A small circuit breaker with Symfony Cache
slides.tldr: Keep the failure count and the "cut until" time in Symfony Cache. While cut, skip the call and go straight to the fallback; otherwise call, and on success reset the count to zero.

blocks.body: You don't need a whole library: one small class is enough. Keep the state (how many failures, and until when it is cut) in the cache. If the cache is Redis, every server sees the same state, so when one server decides the service is sick, all of them know.

marks.tip: If until is in the future, the breaker is OPEN. The fallback returns at once and the network is never touched.
Once until has passed, execution comes through this path: this is half-open. fails is still at the threshold, so a single failure cuts it again.
One success resets the count: it counts consecutive failures, not the total.
Only network failures and 5xx answers count. A 4xx (ClientException) means our own request was wrong, and a bug such as a TypeError is not counted either.
Separate breakers by name: even if courier is cut, the payment breaker runs on its own.
What the fallback should be is a business decision. It is the subject of the next lesson, graceful degradation.

items: Count only network or 5xx failures. If you trip the breaker on 4xx caused by a user's bad input, you will shut off a healthy service.
In half-open this small version can let many requests through as tests at once. With heavy traffic, use Symfony Lock or a dedicated library.
Keep the cache pool in Redis, or each server learns separately. You can use `framework.cache.app` or a dedicated pool.
Send a log and a metric whenever the breaker trips, because it is the best signal that a service is sick.

check.q: In this code the threshold is 5 and openSeconds is 30. When does the 6th call reach the service, and when not?
check.a: After the 5th failure, no call goes through for 30 seconds (OPEN). The first call after those 30 seconds is the test: on success it runs normally, on failure it is blocked for another 30 seconds.

slides.title: Pitfall: retries at every layer, with no retry budget
slides.tldr: 3 retries at each layer means 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 calls. Keep retries in a single layer, and cap retries to a small share of total traffic (a retry budget).

blocks.body: Each layer thinks, for its own good, "let me add a few retries." But retries multiply, they don't add. If the Vue app retries 3 times, the Symfony API 3 times and the gateway client 3 times, one click can mean up to 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 calls. Look at the three layers below.

blocks.caption: One click, three layers, 3 retries each: up to 64 calls at the gateway

layers.label: Vue app
layers.tip: When the browser call fails, it sends again by itself. Every attempt is a new request to the API.

layers.label: Symfony API
layers.tip: For every request, the API may itself call the gateway 4 times. Here 4 × 4 = 16.

layers.label: Gateway client
layers.tip: All the retries below add up to 16 × 4 = 64. The sick gateway takes the most pressure here.

blocks.caption: The same click: retries in every layer, or in one layer only

columns.title: Retries in all 3 layers
items: Vue 4 × API 4 × client 4 attempts
Up to 64 calls reach the sick gateway
columns.tip: Each layer retries on its own, so the counts multiply.

columns.title: Retries in one layer
items: Vue 1 × API 1 × client 4 attempts
At most 4 calls reach the gateway
Price: upper layers fail sooner, so they need a fallback
columns.tip: Only the layer next to the gateway retries. The layers above try once.

marks.tip: The real strategy (GenericRetryStrategy) decides first: is this error retryable at all?
Take a token only if it is retryable. With a token_bucket at 10/second, retries stay at about 10% of 100 rps.

blocks.body: Retries live in one layer, and their budget is about 10% of total traffic.

items: Wire the strategy in with `new RetryableHttpClient($inner, new BudgetedRetryStrategy(new GenericRetryStrategy(), $limiter), 3)`.
When the budget's tokens run out, return the fallback straight away. A breaker and a budget work well together.
Keep the limiter's storage shared (Redis). Otherwise each server gets its own budget and the cap is multiplied by the server count.
A budget only caps retries, it doesn't heal the gateway. Once tokens run out a temporary error goes unretried, so keep a fallback ready.

use: Retry in the lowest layer (the one closest to the gateway)
The upper layers try once, then fail fast or use a fallback
avoid: Retries at every layer "for its own safety"

check.q: Which single layer should hold the retries, and why? And what does a retry budget stop?
check.a: The lowest layer, because it is the one that knows whether an error is temporary, and putting retries higher up multiplies the calls. A budget stops retries from exceeding a small share of total traffic.

slides.title: Recommendations broke, so the whole product page returned 500
slides.tldr: When a minor part fails, killing the whole page is a mistake. Keep the core working, drop the optional part, and the user will barely notice.

blocks.title: A home backup battery during a power outage
blocks.body: When the power goes out, a home backup battery doesn't run the whole house. It runs what was chosen in advance: a few lights, a fan, the fridge. The AC, water heater and oven stay off. The house limps along, but it keeps going. In software this is called **graceful degradation**: when you can't do everything, keep the most important things working.

blocks.caption: The recommendation service is down: the same failure, two different responses

columns.title: Before: all or nothing
items: The recommendation service times out
The exception travels up to the controller
The whole page returns 500: price, images, "Add to cart" all gone
Sales stop, though only decoration was broken
columns.tip: The code assumes every part will succeed. One exception kills the whole request.

columns.title: After: the core survives
items: The recommendation service times out
The code catches it and returns an old list or an empty one
The page opens: price, images and "Add to cart" are there
The user carries on shopping
columns.tip: The code knows which parts are essential and which are not. When an optional part fails, it is quietly dropped.

blocks.body: When an optional part fails, only that part goes, not the whole page.

aside.title: The site that kept only "Add to cart" alive
aside.body: At one e-commerce site, the reviews and recommendations services were down for about an hour. The code had already treated those parts as optional, so product pages opened without reviews. Customers could still buy. The sales graph showed only a slight dip that day.

items.meaning: When some parts break, the system stays up with fewer features instead of collapsing entirely.
A substitute answer when the main way fails: old data, a default value or an empty result.

check.q: Which parts of a product page would you treat as core, and which as optional? Why?
check.a: Core: price, images, "Add to cart", since you can't buy without them. Optional: recommendations, reviews, "how many are viewing", since you can still buy without them.

slides.title: The fallback ladder: if one fails, take the next
slides.tldr: Decide the ladder for each call in advance: live data, then a stale copy, then a default, and finally switch the feature off. But never invent anything to do with money.

blocks.body: Like the backup battery, decide a ladder for every dependency in advance. Step one is live data. If you can't get that, use **stale data**: the last good copy you received. If there is none, use a safe **default**, such as an empty list. Finally, switch the whole feature off and tell the user. The lower you go, the less precise the answer, but the less the site collapses.

blocks.caption: The fallback ladder: step down from the top, best option first

layers.label: 1. Live data
layers.tip: The best and freshest answer. Staying here is the goal.

layers.label: 2. Stale copy
layers.sub: the last good answer, a few hours old
layers.tip: The last successful answer kept in the cache. For recommendations or a catalog, it is almost as good.

layers.label: 3. A default value
layers.sub: empty, a popular list, a rate fixed in advance
layers.tip: A safe answer the business has approved in advance. Not something made up on the spot.

layers.label: 4. Feature off
layers.sub: hide the part or write "not available now"
layers.tip: The kill switch. The more dangerous the feature, the earlier this step comes.

blocks.title: Where you must not step down the ladder
items: Guessing money data such as a balance, stock or price
Saying "success" without knowing whether a payment went through
Saying "fine, come in" when a permission check fails

blocks.body: On failure you may give an old or empty answer, but never a wrong one when money or permissions are involved.

aside.body: Live, stale, default, off: write these four steps down in advance for every dependency.

use: Slow-changing data such as a catalog or config

items.label: The breaker decides when to step down

check.q: The balance service fails when showing a customer's balance. Is it right to show a stale copy, or to switch the feature off?
check.a: Switch it off, or show a clear "can't show this right now". If money data is out of date, the customer may make a wrong decision. Stale copies are only for slow-changing data.

slides.title: A stale copy and a kill switch in Symfony
slides.tldr: Keep every successful answer in the cache as the last good copy. On failure serve it, or an empty list, and flag degraded: true in the response. Keep core data and optional parts separate.

blocks.body: The rule: every time a successful answer arrives, store it in the cache for a day as the "last good copy". On failure, serve that copy, or an empty list if there is none. And send a `degraded` flag with the response, so the frontend knows what to show.

marks.tip: Only the unreliable call goes in the try. On success the copy is rewritten fresh.
expiresAfter(86400): one day. Recommendations older than that have no value, so the cache will drop them itself.
Logging the failure matters: otherwise recommendations could be a month old and nobody would know.
degraded: true doesn't lie to the user. The frontend can show a small note.
The core data is not in a try/catch here. If the price can't be loaded, a 500 is right; showing a wrong price is not.
The kill switch is just a cache key here. If the service gets terribly slow, you can switch it off without even calling it. No deploy needed.

blocks.body: Calls for optional parts always go in try/catch, calls for core parts never do.

items: Prepare a tiny console command that runs `$cache->save($cache->getItem('kill.recommendations')->set(true))`. In a crisis there is no time to write code.
Use a separate cache key for the stale copy. If it sits under a key with a short TTL, expiry will delete the last good copy too.
Catching everything with catch (\Throwable) quietly buries bugs in your own code too. Catch the specific ExceptionInterface.

check.q: In the controller, the product call is not in a try/catch but the recommendations call is. Why the asymmetry?
check.a: Product data is core: without it you can't buy, so an honest failure is the right answer. Recommendations are optional: the page works without them, so they can be dropped.

slides.title: A degraded UI in Vue: tell the user honestly
slides.tldr: Make core and optional calls separately (Promise.allSettled). If the optional one fails the page carries on, with a short honest note or an alternative link. If the core one fails, show an error with a retry button.

blocks.body: The most common frontend mistake is `await Promise.all([api.product(id), api.recommendations(id)])`: if recommendations fail, the product you already received is thrown away too, and the page shows an error. `Promise.allSettled` reports each result separately, so you decide which failure kills the page and which only costs one part.

marks.tip: allSettled never rejects. Each result comes back as { status, value | reason }.
Only when the core call fails does the whole page show an error. This decision is made in advance.
If recommendations fail: an empty list and degraded: true. The page keeps working.
When showing a stale copy, add an honest note: the user knows the information may be a bit old.
If there is nothing at all, don't leave an empty gap. Offer another route: a link to popular products.

blocks.caption: Four states, and what the user sees in each

rows.tip: The normal state. degraded: false.

cells: Recommendations + "may be slightly out of date"
rows.tip: Things keep working, and the user is told the truth too.

cells: "Not available now" + a popular products link
rows.tip: The part is gone, but the user isn't stuck: there is a way forward.
This is the only state where the whole page fails. The retry button lets the user try again on their own.

items: Test the degraded UI yourself: block the network in devtools or use a mock, and run through each state once.
Write failure messages in the user's language: not "Error 503" but "Recommendations are unavailable right now".

aside.body: Don't leave the user in the dark: say what they are missing, and what they can do now.

check.q: Why Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all, and the failure of which call should make the whole page show an error?
check.a: Promise.all discards everything when one call fails. allSettled gives each result separately, so only a failure of the core (product) call shows an error, and a recommendations failure leaves the page working.

slides.title: Pitfall: the fallback that quietly lies
slides.tldr: In money-related calls, `catch → return 0` is the most dangerous fallback. A good one is a value approved in advance, logged, and not dependent on the very thing that failed.

blocks.body: Hiding every failure is not degradation. When the courier fails to return a delivery charge, the code below quietly returns 0. For a whole day every order shipped with no delivery charge, and nobody noticed. A proper fallback is decided in advance by someone, logged, and honest with the user. For money, the only safe default is a number the business approved beforehand and shown as an estimate. The price: the customer may pay a little more than the real charge, so settle the difference once the courier is back.

marks.tip: \Throwable catches everything, bugs in your own code included. Nothing is logged and no metric moves.
Here 0 is a lie standing in for "I don't know". The money comes straight out of the company's pocket.
Only HttpClient errors are caught. Bugs such as a TypeError rise up as before and show in the logs.
With a log you can tell how often the fallback ran. Add an alert, and the problem is caught in minutes, not hours.
A number chosen in advance: someone thought it through and approved it. You can show the customer an "estimated charge".

blocks.title: Three conditions for a good fallback
items: Decided in advance: the business knows and agreed, and the code did not guess
Visible: there is a log, a metric and an alert, never silent
Independent: the fallback does not depend on the dependency that failed
A fallback you never test will run for the first time on the day of the crisis, and that is when it will break. Switch off a dependency on purpose at regular intervals to check.
If a fallback goes to the same database or cache that has failed, it is not a fallback, it is the same trap.

items.label: Failing on purpose to test (game day)

check.q: Why is the maximum zone rate a better courier fallback than `return 0`?
check.a: The business approved that rate in advance, so the company doesn't lose money. 0 passes off "I don't know" as "free", and quietly loses money.

slides.title: During a deploy, old code meets a new database
slides.tldr: A deploy is not instant. For a few minutes old and new code run side by side on the same database, so renaming one column can send users a 500.

blocks.title: Installing a new espresso machine at the coffee shop
blocks.body: The owner of a coffee shop wants to replace the old espresso machine with a new one. If he closes the shop, customers go to another one. So a smart owner sets up the new machine next to it first, tries it out, moves the customers over, and only then removes the old one. During the switch both machines serve customers at once. Code works the same way: in a **zero-downtime deploy**, the old and new versions run together for a while.

blocks.caption: Rolling deploy: the new server ran the migration while the old server is still serving customers

actors.label: User
actors.tip: They have no idea a deploy is running. For them the site should always be open.

actors.label: Old server (v1)
actors.tip: Still running the old code. It reads the `phone` column.

actors.label: New server (v2)
actors.tip: The new code, which uses the `mobile` column. It went live first.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: There is only one database and both versions use it. The root of all the trouble is here.

messages.label: migration: the phone column becomes mobile
messages.tip: RENAME COLUMN happens in an instant, but the old code is still running.

messages.note: There is no column called phone now

messages.label: ERROR: column phone does not exist

blocks.body: While a deploy runs, old and new code share one database. So never rename in one step: add the new, move over, then drop the old.

aside.title: The Friday evening deploy
aside.body: A team renamed a column on a Friday evening and called it a "2-minute deploy". The rolling deploy took 8 minutes to finish. For those 8 minutes the old servers returned a 500 on every profile request, and roughly 200 users a minute abandoned checkout.

items.meaning: Rolling out a new version without the site being down at any point.
A new change that still works fine with the old code.

check.q: The deploy takes only 2 minutes. Why does renaming a column still cause trouble?
check.a: For those two minutes (or more) the old servers are still running. They look for the column under its old name, which no longer exists in the database, so they error.

slides.title: Three ways: rolling, blue/green, canary
slides.tldr: Rolling replaces servers one at a time, blue/green switches to a whole new environment, canary tests on a small slice first. In all three, two versions run together for a while.

blocks.body: Back to the coffee shop. **Rolling**: replace the machines one by one. **Blue/green**: set up a whole new shop next door, send every customer there in a single moment, and keep the old one ready. **Canary**: let just a few people taste one cup of the new blend, and serve everyone if it goes well.

blocks.caption: Blue/green: switch once Green is up and tested, and keep Blue as the way back

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.tip: The switch lives here. It decides whether traffic goes to Blue or to Green.

nodes.label: Blue (v1)
nodes.tip: The version that is live right now. It is not shut down even after the switch.

nodes.label: Green (v2)
nodes.tip: The new version, on separate servers. It is fully tested before it gets any traffic.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Both environments use the same database, so the schema has to suit both versions.

edges.label: All traffic goes to Blue (v1) right now
Green (v2) starts up and passes health checks, but gets no traffic
Green runs smoke tests against the same database
The switch: all traffic moves to Green
If there is a problem, the switch goes back to Blue
edges.tip: This is the strength of blue/green: rollback just means flipping the switch back, not deploying again.

blocks.caption: The three strategies compared

cells: Replaces one server at a time
New version on a small slice first
rows.tip: All three end up giving everyone the new version. They differ only in how they spread the risk.
Blue/green is expensive on rented servers, but in the cloud it is cheap to rent for a few minutes.

cells: Quick: pull back the small slice
rows.tip: The speed of rollback decides how big the damage is when something goes wrong.

cells: Everyone moves at the moment of the switch
rows.tip: A canary only works if you can read the error rate and latency properly.
Most teams start with rolling, then add canary or blue/green for risky work.

blocks.body: Whichever strategy you use, old and new code run side by side during the deploy: every release must be backward compatible.

use: Rolling: small daily changes, when you want low cost
Blue/green: big changes, when you need fast rollback
Canary: risky features, tested on real traffic
avoid: Canary: if you have no way to measure the error rate

items.meaning: A short test, right after startup, that checks a few core actions (login, add to cart) actually work.
Like the canary in a coal mine: the new version first gets a small slice of traffic, and if something is wrong, that slice tells you first.

check.q: Which strategy has the fastest rollback, and why?
check.a: Blue/green: the old environment (Blue) is still up and ready. You just flip the load balancer switch back, and nothing needs to be deployed again.

slides.title: Expand-contract: the safe way to change a column
slides.tldr: Not in one go but across several releases: add the new column (expand), write to both, backfill old rows, move reads to the new one, and drop the old one last (contract). At every step old code survives.

blocks.body: The `phone` column has to become `mobile`. Instead of a single rename, do it like setting up the new machine next to the old: first add the new column (**expand**), and only after everything has moved over, drop the old one (**contract**). Each step is its own release, so at every step both old and new code keep working. The order matters, and the next slide shows why.

blocks.caption: From phone to mobile: five steps, in this order, each its own release or run

steps.title: 1. Expand
steps.body: Add a nullable mobile column. The code doesn't change.
steps.tip: Adding a column is always safe: old code doesn't even know the new column exists.

steps.title: 2. Write to both
steps.body: Release code that writes phone and mobile.
steps.tip: Wait for the rollout to end: servers still on the old code write only phone.

steps.title: 3. Backfill
steps.body: Once step 2 is fully live, copy phone into the old rows, in batches.
steps.tip: The next slide has the command, and shows why this must come after step 2.

steps.title: 4. Move reads
steps.body: Release code that reads mobile. Keep writing both.
steps.tip: Keep writing phone for now: if this release is rolled back, the old code still finds fresh numbers in phone.

steps.title: 5. Contract
steps.body: Stop using phone in code. Drop the column in a later release.
steps.tip: The only step you can't undo. Code first, the drop later, and take a backup before it.

marks.tip: No NOT NULL, and DEFAULT NULL: in PostgreSQL this is instant and doesn't lock the table. Old INSERTs keep working too.
Old servers still read phone. To make sure the new number reaches them, it is written to phone too.
If the new column is empty, show the old one. Once the backfill is done, this fallback is no longer needed.

blocks.body: Never change a column or table in a single release: add first, and drop only after everyone has moved.

items: Adding a NOT NULL column with no default breaks INSERTs from old code. Keep it nullable first, and add the constraint after the backfill.
On a big table, one UPDATE holds locks on every row. Run the backfill in batches of 1,000 rows.
The price: one rename becomes five steps over several days, with two columns living side by side.

use: Any column or table that live users read or write while you deploy
avoid: A small internal tool where 10 minutes of planned downtime is fine: five steps cost more
A rename you can skip by simply keeping the old name

check.q: Why does expand-contract take five steps instead of a rename? Which step can't be undone?
check.a: At every step both the old and the new version run fine, so nothing breaks in the middle of a deploy. Only the last step (contract), dropping the column, can't be undone.

slides.title: Backfill in the right order, in small batches
slides.tldr: Dual-write goes live first, the backfill runs after that rollout ends, a check proves no gaps remain, and only then do reads move. Copy in batches; the command is safe to re-run.

blocks.body: Say the `user` table has 10,000 rows and rolling out the new code takes 2 minutes. The order is not a matter of taste: each step makes the next one safe. Look at what happens to new sign-ups when the backfill (copying old values into the new column) runs too early.

blocks.caption: The same two steps, in the wrong and in the right order

columns.title: Backfill first
items: The backfill copies the 10,000 existing users
Until the write-to-both release goes out, 300 more sign up: saved to phone only
Reads move to mobile: those 300 users show no number, and nothing ever fixes it
columns.tip: The copy happens while the old code is still saving everything to phone only.

columns.title: Write-to-both first
items: Release write-to-both. During the 2-minute rollout, old servers save about 40 rows to phone only
When the rollout has ended, the backfill copies those 40 and the 10,000 old rows
Check that zero rows are left, then move reads
columns.tip: From the moment the rollout ends, every save fills both columns. The backfill only has to cover the past.

marks.tip: Only rows not yet copied are picked. That is what makes the command safe to stop, restart or run twice.
Each batch holds its locks for milliseconds. One UPDATE over millions of rows would hold them for minutes and stall sign-ups.
The loop ends when a round copies nothing: no row is left to copy.

blocks.code:
-- must return 0 before reads move to mobile
SELECT count(*) FROM "user" WHERE mobile IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL;

marks.tip: Counts rows that have a number in phone but nothing in mobile. Anything above 0 means a gap that would show up as a missing number.

items.desc: Copies phone into mobile, 1,000 rows at a time, until none are left

items: Do not start the backfill while the write-to-both rollout is still running: old servers keep adding phone-only rows.
The price: the table is busier for the duration, and the pause makes it slower on purpose. Run it off-peak.
Do not add NOT NULL on mobile until the check returns 0 and nothing writes only phone.

check.q: Nicole runs the backfill first and releases write-to-both an hour later. What goes wrong, and for whom?
check.a: Everyone who signed up in that hour is saved to phone only, so after reads move to mobile they show no number. Write-to-both first, then backfill, closes that gap.

slides.title: Shut the old server down politely
slides.tldr: Take the old server off the load balancer, then send the stop signal that means "finish up": SIGQUIT for php-fpm, SIGTERM for a Messenger worker. php-fpm stops on the spot if it gets SIGTERM.

blocks.body: At the coffee shop, before you take away the old machine you let the drinks already started be finished, or the customer's drink gets dropped. A server is the same: shut it down abruptly and the requests in flight are cut off halfway. One trap hides in the signal: php-fpm treats SIGTERM as "stop now". A 30-second report running when the container is told to stop is killed on the spot, and the user gets a 502. Only SIGQUIT makes php-fpm finish first.

blocks.caption: The polite order for shutting down a server

steps.title: 1. Take it off the line
steps.body: The load balancer stops sending new requests to this server.
steps.tip: On Kubernetes this starts as soon as the pod is marked terminating. The news takes seconds to reach every load balancer, hence the short wait (preStop) in the config below.

steps.title: 2. Send the right signal
steps.body: php-fpm needs SIGQUIT. A Messenger worker needs SIGTERM.
steps.tip: php-fpm treats SIGTERM as "stop now" and cuts requests in flight. SIGQUIT means "finish current requests, then exit". A Messenger worker handles SIGTERM itself.

steps.title: 3. Finish work in progress
steps.body: Current requests and messages finish, and nothing new is taken.
steps.tip: A Messenger worker finishes its current message and only then stops (this needs the pcntl extension). php-fpm lets each worker complete its current request.

steps.title: 4. A time limit
steps.body: Say 45 seconds. If it hasn't stopped by then...
steps.tip: The limit should be longer than the longest request or message in your system.

steps.title: 5. SIGKILL
steps.body: ...it is killed by force. This is the last resort.
steps.tip: SIGKILL can't be caught. Work in progress is lost, so you don't want to get this far.

blocks.code:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: app
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 2
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: { command: ['sleep', '10'] }

marks.tip: This many seconds are allowed after the stop signal, then SIGKILL. Set it longer than your longest request.

If this URL fails, the orchestrator stops sending that pod new requests. Check only what the app truly can't run without, like the database: a slow external courier API here would pull every server off the line.
Wait 10 seconds before the stop signal: in that time the load balancers drop the server from their lists.

blocks.code:
FROM php:8.3-fpm-alpine

# php-fpm: SIGTERM = stop now, cutting requests in flight.
# SIGQUIT = finish the current requests, then exit.
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT
# how long the master waits for workers to finish after SIGQUIT
RUN printf '[global]\nprocess_control_timeout = 40s\n' \
    > /usr/local/etc/php-fpm.d/zz-shutdown.conf

COPY . /var/www/html

marks.tip: The key line. Docker and Kubernetes send this signal instead of SIGTERM when the container stops. The official php-fpm image already sets it; a custom base image may not.
Without this, the master waits almost nothing for its workers after SIGQUIT, and a long request is still cut. Keep it below terminationGracePeriodSeconds (45).

blocks.body: php-fpm: SIGTERM stops now, SIGQUIT finishes first.

items.desc: Stops itself politely after an hour or 128MB, and the supervisor starts it again
After a deploy, tells running workers to finish their last message and stop, then restart on the new code

items: During a deploy the workers are running old code too. If you don't run messenger:stop-workers, they stay on the old code.
A message cut off halfway goes back on the queue. So keep handlers idempotent, so that running twice does no harm.
Test it once: start a request that sleeps 20 seconds, stop the container, and check the request still completes.

items.label: What happens when a message arrives twice

check.q: In a rolling deploy, why take the old server off the load balancer first, and why does php-fpm need SIGQUIT?
check.a: Without the first, new requests keep arriving while it shuts down. On SIGTERM php-fpm cuts the requests in flight; only SIGQUIT lets them finish.

slides.title: Pitfall: you can roll code back, but not data
slides.tldr: If a release drops a column, rolling the code back no longer helps: the old code can't run. To keep rollback safe, release migrations and code separately, and write the plan in advance.

blocks.body: When the error rate jumps after a deploy, our first thought is "go back to the previous version". But rolling code back is easy, and rolling a database back is nearly impossible. If the same release dropped the `phone` column, the old code will crash against the new database even after you roll back.

marks.tip: Dropping the column in the same release as the code change: the rolled-back old code won't find this column.
down() does bring the column back, but not the numbers that were in it. This is not a real rollback.

blocks.caption: The same bad release, with the drop in the same release and in a later one

columns.title: Same release
items: Deploy the new code and DROP phone together
Errors rise, so you roll the code back
The old code asks for phone, which is gone: still failing
down() brings back an empty column, the numbers are lost
columns.tip: Code change and DROP COLUMN go out together. Rolling back only undoes half of it.

columns.title: Separate releases
items: Release 1: the code stops using phone, the column stays
Errors rise: roll the code back in seconds, phone is intact
A week later all is calm: drop phone in its own release, after a backup
columns.tip: The risky code change goes alone. If it fails, the data is still there to go back to.

columns.title: What it costs
items: A dead column lingers for days
One change needs two releases, and someone must remember the second
Skip it for a throwaway table nobody reads
columns.tip: The safe way has a price. Know it, and plan the second release so it is not forgotten.

blocks.title: Five conditions for a rollback plan
items: The previous version's artifact is built and kept, and can be started with one command
Every migration is compatible with the old code (expand only, contract in a separate release)
Risky features sit behind a feature flag, so undoing them needs no deploy
A trigger decided in advance: for example, roll back within 5 minutes if 5xx passes 1%
The rollback has been rehearsed once before you need it

blocks.body: A deploy without a rollback plan is not a deploy, it is a gamble.

items: "We'll fix it with a hotfix" is not a rollback. Spotting the mistake, writing the code and deploying it takes several times longer.
Migrations that change data (a backfill) can't be undone. So make sure a backup exists before you run them.

check.q: A release shipped the new code together with "DROP COLUMN phone". Why doesn't rolling back solve it?
check.a: Even when the code goes back, the column is gone. The old code will fail trying to read phone, and down() restores only the column, not the data inside it.

slides.title: The whole region is down, and the backup is in it
slides.tldr: If the app, database and backup are all in one region, a single disaster takes everything. A disaster plan means preparing a way back somewhere else in advance.

blocks.title: The store owner's account book
blocks.body: Every night the store owner photocopies the account book (the book where she writes down who owes what) and keeps the copy in the store's own drawer. One day the store catches fire. The original book burns, and so does the photocopy, because both were in the same place. And she has no idea where she will trade tomorrow. If your database and backup sit in one region, you are in exactly the same position.

blocks.caption: Everything in one region: no way back after a disaster, unless a copy lives elsewhere

nodes.label: Users
nodes.tip: All they know is that the site won't open. They have no need to know why.

nodes.label: Region A
nodes.tip: A data center in Virginia, or one cloud region. Everything runs here.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.tip: Taken every night, but kept in storage in the same region. If the region goes, so does this.

nodes.label: Region B
nodes.tip: There is another place, but it has no code, no database and no plan.

edges.label: All traffic goes to a single region
Every night the backup goes to storage in the same region
Region A is down: the app and the backup are both unreachable, and there is no response for 6 hours
No way back: nothing is set up in Region B
The fix: also copy the backup to Region B every night, so a way back exists

blocks.body: If the place a backup depends on goes, the backup goes with it. Keep a copy in another region and another account.

aside.title: A fire in the data center
aside.body: A fire broke out in one data center of a large cloud provider and took many customers' servers offline. Customers whose backups were in another data center or region were back within the day. Some of the rest never got their data back.

items.meaning: A cluster of data centers in a geographically separate area, such as Virginia or Oregon. When one region fails, another usually survives.
The plan and setup for bringing a system back after a major disaster (a region down, data deleted).

check.q: The nightly backup is taken every day, yet it was no use in a regional disaster. What is the likely reason?
check.a: The backup was kept in the same region, so it went down with the region. Backups must be kept in a different region.

slides.title: RPO and RTO: how much we lose, how long we are down
slides.tldr: RPO is the most data (measured in time) you can afford to lose, and RTO is the longest you can afford to be down. The business sets both, and the lower you want them, the more they cost.

blocks.body: The store fire makes it easy to see. Whatever was written in the account book after the last photocopy is lost: that span of time is the **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective). And the time it takes for the store to open again is the **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective). An objective is a limit you set in advance, not a number you read off after the event.

blocks.caption: The timeline of one disaster: 7 minutes of data lost, 83 minutes down

steps.title: 10:00 last backup
steps.body: Anything written from now on exists only in the main database.
steps.tip: The more frequent the backup or replication, the closer this point sits to the disaster.

steps.title: 10:07 disaster
steps.body: The region goes down. Seven minutes of data, from 10:00 to 10:07, is lost.
steps.tip: Those 7 minutes are the data actually lost. If the limit (RPO) was lower than this, the target was missed.

steps.body: Recovery work: restore the backup, start the app, move the traffic.
steps.tip: During this time users can do nothing.

steps.title: 11:30 back up
steps.body: Down for 83 minutes in total. This is the actual recovery time this time.
steps.tip: If the limit (RTO) was 60 minutes, the target was missed this time, and the gap has to be fixed before the next drill.

blocks.caption: Different RPO and RTO for different work, by importance

rows.tip: Losing money data does direct harm. This needs continuous replication and fast failover, and that is the most expensive option.
If a few minutes of orders are lost, customers can order again. That is tolerable.
The nightly backup is enough. These can be rebuilt.

blocks.body: The business sets RPO and RTO, not the engineer. The lower you want them, the more they cost.

aside.body: RPO = how much data is gone (look backwards). RTO = how long we are down (look forwards).

items.meaning: The most data, measured in time, that the business will accept losing.
The longest the business will tolerate between a disaster and being back up.
A second copy of the database that is kept up to date continuously, so it is only seconds behind.
Switching users from the broken system to the standby one.

check.q: Backups are taken once every 24 hours. What can your RPO be at most, and why is that not enough for payments?
check.a: Up to 24 hours: if the disaster hits just before the backup, a whole day of data is gone. That is unacceptable for payments, so you need continuous replication.

slides.title: Two branches: active-passive vs active-active
slides.tldr: Active-passive: the second region stands ready, and traffic moves there in a disaster. Active-active: both regions serve traffic, but reconciling data written in two places is the truly hard part. Cheaper options come next.

blocks.body: Say the store has two branches, in Chicago and Dallas. **Active-passive**: the Dallas branch only waits, receives copies of Chicago's account book, and takes over if Chicago closes. **Active-active**: both branches serve customers. But if the same customer's credit is written differently in the two branches, it can't be reconciled later. That is a conflict.

blocks.caption: The two patterns side by side

columns.title: Active-passive
items: One region serves traffic, the other stands ready
Data is replicated from the main region to the other (async)
In a disaster the other becomes primary and DNS is moved
RTO: minutes to hours, RPO: the replication lag
Lower cost: the standby region can be smaller
columns.tip: The right start for most systems. It is simple, because writes happen in one place only.

columns.title: Active-active
items: Both regions handle reads and writes
Data replicates both ways, and conflicts must be reconciled
If one goes down the other is already running, so RTO is nearly zero
Answers come from the region closest to the user: lower latency
The highest cost and complexity
columns.tip: It gives fast failover and low latency, but handling data conflicts is one of the hardest problems in engineering.

blocks.title: What you must settle in multi-region
items: Who moves the traffic: DNS or a global load balancer, with a short DNS TTL
How big the replication lag is: this is your real RPO, so measure it
Where writes go: one region or two
Whether sessions, cache, file storage and secrets exist in the other region

blocks.body: Before choosing active-active, ask yourself: do I really need to write in two places?

use: Active-passive: most businesses, where an RTO of minutes to hours is tolerable
Active-active: a global user base, or when you want an RTO near zero
avoid: Active-active: a small team on a limited budget, when active-passive is enough

items.meaning: How far the copy trails the main database. That much data is lost if the main one dies right now.
How many seconds the world may remember a site's address. A long TTL slows the move to another region.
Two regions saved different values for the same thing, and one must win.

items.label: The clash between consistency and availability

check.q: In active-active, what happens when the same user's address is changed two different ways in two regions at once, and why is that not a problem in active-passive?
check.a: The two regions write two different values and create a conflict, which needs a rule to reconcile. In active-passive, writes happen in only one region, so there is no conflict at all.

slides.title: The cheaper rungs: backup-and-restore and pilot light
slides.tldr: Between nothing and a standby region sit two cheaper options: backup-and-restore (copies only, rebuilt after a disaster) and pilot light (only the database kept running). Pick the cheapest rung that meets your RPO and RTO.

blocks.body: Back to the store. **Backup and restore**: a photocopy of the account book sits in a locker in Dallas. After a fire you rent a new store, copy the book over and restock the shelves, which takes a day. **Pilot light**: a small room in Dallas where one assistant copies Chicago's account book all day. The shelves are empty and the lights are off, but the ledger is current, so reopening takes an hour or two.

blocks.caption: The four options, from cheapest to dearest

rows.tip: You pay only for storage and the transfer between regions. Everything else is built after the disaster.

cells: Database replica only, app switched off
rows.tip: The data is always current. The wait is for starting the app servers.

cells: A small full copy, already running
rows.tip: This is the active-passive pattern of the last slide. The app is already up, so recovery is a traffic move plus a scale-up.
Both regions serve users all the time, and conflicts must be reconciled.

blocks.caption: Rough extra monthly cost, as a share of Region A's bill (an illustration; your numbers will differ)

items.label: Backup and restore
items.tip: Storage for the copies, plus the transfer between regions.

items.label: Pilot light
items.tip: A database replica running all the time, plus its network traffic.

items.label: Warm standby
items.tip: Everything running, at a fraction of full size.

items.label: Active-active
items.tip: A second full-size copy, plus the engineering work of resolving conflicts.

blocks.code:
# Pilot light: only the database replica runs in Region B. Start the rest.
# 1. The replica becomes the primary
psql -h replica.region-b -c "SELECT pg_promote();"

# 2. Scale the app up from 0 to full size
kubectl --context region-b scale deployment/app --replicas=6
kubectl --context region-b scale deployment/worker --replicas=2

# 3. Wait until it is ready (a few minutes), then move the traffic
