kubectl --context region-b rollout status deployment/app --timeout=600s

marks.tip: This is what the pilot light pays for in RTO: starting servers takes minutes. A warm standby skips this step because the app already runs.

blocks.body: Buy only the recovery speed the business needs: the cheapest rung that meets RPO and RTO.

use: Backup and restore: reports, internal tools, anything that can be down for a day
Pilot light: orders and carts, where an hour or two down is tolerable
avoid: Backup and restore on a big database: 200 GB at 50 GB an hour is 4 hours of restore before the app starts
Pilot light when you need minutes, not hours: starting servers takes time

items: Switched-off parts rot. Deploy every release to Region B too, even with the app at zero copies, and test the scale-up in a game day.
Copies sent to Region B should live in a separate account too, or one mistake deletes both.

items.meaning: Like the small flame on a gas stove: only the essential part (the data) stays on, and the rest is lit when needed.
A smaller but complete copy of the system, already running and ready to be scaled up.

check.q: A 200 GB database is restored from backup at 50 GB an hour. How long does the restore alone take, and what does that say about backup-and-restore for a 2-hour RTO?
check.a: 4 hours, before the app even starts. It misses a 2-hour RTO, so you need a replica already running in the other region (pilot light or better).

slides.title: Game day: break things on purpose to test
slides.tldr: A DR plan you haven't tested is only a hope. On a chosen day, run a failover on purpose, measure the real RPO and RTO, and fix whatever turns out wrong.

blocks.body: It is like a fire drill: everyone knows the way out before the fire starts. In a **game day**, the team picks a day and, with everyone aware, causes a failure on purpose and runs the whole recovery path. The aim is not to find someone to blame but to find the gaps.

blocks.caption: The six steps of a game day

steps.title: 1. Set the goal
steps.body: RPO 1 minute, RTO 30 minutes. This is the pass/fail mark.
steps.tip: Write the limits down before the drill starts, or afterwards you can call it "good enough".

steps.title: 2. Write the runbook
steps.body: Step by step who does what, with commands.
steps.tip: A good runbook is one that even a newcomer can follow when the usual person is on leave.

steps.title: 3. Cause the failure
steps.body: In staging first. Later, in a controlled way in production at low traffic.
steps.tip: Build confidence in staging, then production. In production, keep someone watching and the stop switch in hand.

steps.title: 4. Run the recovery
steps.body: Following the runbook, with timing.
steps.tip: Any step where someone gets stuck or has to guess is a gap in the runbook.

steps.title: 5. Measure
steps.body: The real RPO and RTO, compared with the goal.
steps.tip: The most useful numbers: how long it really took this time, and how much data was lost.

steps.title: 6. Fix
steps.body: A list of gaps, with owners and dates.
steps.tip: A drill pays off only when its gaps are fixed before the next drill.

blocks.code:
# 1. How far behind is the replica? This is the actual RPO right now
psql -h replica.region-b -c \
  "SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag;"

# 2. Promote the replica to be the new primary
psql -h replica.region-b -c "SELECT pg_promote();"

# 3. Confirm: if false, it is no longer a replica and can take writes
psql -h replica.region-b -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"

# 4. Region B's app already points at replica.region-b, so no config changes.
# Restart it so it opens fresh connections and the workers start clean
kubectl --context region-b rollout restart deployment/app deployment/worker

marks.tip: In a real failure, when the primary dies this lag is the limit on lost data. Measure it first during the drill and check it is within the RPO target.
pg_promote() is available from PostgreSQL 12. The replica opens up for writes. Never bring the old primary back up, or you get a split brain.
Region B's app was configured with the replica's address from the start, so there is no URL to change in the middle of a disaster. Time this step in the drill and write it into the runbook.

blocks.body: A recovery that has never been run is a recovery you can't assume will work.

items: Something will break in your first game day: the password isn't in the other region, the DNS TTL is 24 hours, the runbook is out of date. That is the whole point.
Hands-on drills are a good start before chaos tooling (such as cutting the network).
If the old primary suddenly returns, you end up with two primaries (split brain). Stop it or isolate it first.

items.label: What you can show less of during a disaster

check.q: The game day took 83 minutes and the RTO was 60. What should you call it instead of a failure, and what comes next?
check.a: A successful drill: the gap was found before a real incident. Now find which step took the longest, fix it, and run the drill again.

slides.title: Pitfall: it's on paper, but it doesn't work in real life
slides.tldr: A paper DR plan almost always fails: the backup is in the same place, the restore was never tested, the secrets aren't in the other region, the DNS TTL is huge. Catch these in advance.

blocks.body: "We have a DR plan" sounds reassuring. But a plan that has never been run is a paper boat. The four most common problems on disaster day are on the left below, and their fixes on the right.

blocks.caption: A paper plan vs a tested plan

columns.title: Paper DR
items: A backup exists, but nobody has seen a restore
The backup is in the same region and the same account
Secrets and API keys exist only in the main region
DNS TTL is 24 hours: moving takes a day
The runbook is two years old and its author has left
columns.tip: Every assumption is taken as true, and nobody has checked.

columns.title: Tested DR
items: Restores are run regularly and the data checked
The backup is in a different region and a different account
Secrets are stored in both regions and tested
DNS TTL is 60 seconds, and traffic was moved in a drill
The runbook is updated after every drill
columns.tip: Every assumption has been verified in a drill, and the results are written down as numbers.

blocks.body: A backup you have never restored is not a backup, it is a hope.

items: If the backup sits in one account and is deleted by mistake or by a hack, everything is lost. Keep backups in a separate account and make them immutable (undeletable).
If the DR knowledge lives in one person's head, everything stops when they go on leave. Write it in the runbook.
The price of a tested plan: a drill takes a few people a day or two each quarter, and secrets in two regions are two places to protect. Still far cheaper than learning it on disaster day.

aside.body: Backup somewhere else, restore tested, secrets alongside, DNS fast, runbook fresh.

check.q: A backup exists, yet getting back up in the new region got stuck during a disaster. What "paper DR" causes might there be?
check.a: The restore was never tested, the secrets aren't in the other region, a big DNS TTL delayed the traffic move, the runbook was out of date. Each of these would have shown up in a drill.
